body:
Sean Gallagher: starting a thread on the remediation SLA mapping debate from today’s sync. Specifically: Sev1 routing/control-plane vs Sev1 runtime crash. We need crisp TTM/TTR targets that are realistic for on-call + match customer expectations.

Aisha Bello: thx. Quick framing so we’re aligned on terms:
- TTM = time to mitigate (service restored / impact materially reduced)
- TTR = time to permanent fix (merged + deployed OR config change rolled out + verified, not just “we think it’s fixed”)

Aisha Bello: current draft table has Sev1 Routing Degraded = TTM 15m / TTR 72h. Sev1 Runtime Crash = TTM 30m / TTR 5bd. People pushed back both directions.

Mina Haddad: from routing side: if we call something “routing” Sev1, it often manifests as widespread 5xx/timeouts. We *can* mitigate in <15m in the common cases (disable a policy rule, flip fallback, reduce load via rate-limit). But the hard part is sometimes we don’t know it’s routing vs runtime vs fleet yet.

Sean Gallagher: yeah that’s my concern. During declare we’ll have “symptoms” not root cause. If we lock ourselves into an aggressive TTM for “routing” but classify late, metrics get messy.

Mateo Alvarez: on runtime: a “crash” can mean 3 different things:
1) process crashlooping on a model build -> mitigation = rollback model / swap variant / drain pool
2) kernel regression causing hangs -> mitigation might be disable feature flag / revert deploy
3) scheduler bug causing deadlock -> mitigation varies, sometimes restart helps, sometimes not

Mateo Alvarez: for #1 and #2, 30m TTM is fine. For #3, if it’s a novel deadlock, 30m is optimistic if it’s across multiple regions.

Priya Natarajan: we need to separate “mitigation lever exists” vs “requires engineering fix to restore.” Routing/control plane typically has explicit levers (fallback, regional shift, policy toggle). Runtime sometimes does, sometimes doesn’t.

Rachel Kim: adding customer lens: for Enterprise (Dedicated + some Hosted enterprise tiers), they expect:
- acknowledgement in minutes
- a credible ETA within ~30m for Sev1
- frequent updates (15–30m)
They don’t necessarily care if it’s routing vs runtime, they care whether we can *stabilize* quickly.

Dev Patel: support POV: during an active escalation we need an answer to “when will it stop timing out?” If we set routing Sev1 TTM=15m and runtime Sev1 TTM=30m, CS will communicate different expectations… but we often won’t know which bucket we’re in until 20m in.

Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers also have “impact tolerance” differences. Some are okay with degraded throughput if latency is stable; others treat any elevated error rate as Sev1. If we do tier-based SLAs, we should define which tiers map to which comms expectations.

Aisha Bello: proposing we reframe to: TTM targets by *customer tier* + *impact type* more than “component.” But we still need categories for ownership + trend reporting.

Sean Gallagher: can we do this without exploding taxonomy complexity? Remember constraint: low cognitive load during incident.

Mina Haddad: what if we keep categories, but set the same Sev1 TTM target for both routing + runtime and define “TTM = either restore OR engage a documented mitigation plan”?

Priya Natarajan: careful. “Engage a plan” can be gamed. We need something measurable.

Mateo Alvarez: maybe define mitigation as *customer-visible improvement* (e.g., error rate down below X, p95 latency back within Y% of baseline). Otherwise it’s too subjective.

Aisha Bello: yup. For Hosted, we can use SLO burn-rate / 5xx rate and set “mitigated” criteria. For Dedicated, we can use pool-level success rate + queue depth.

Sean Gallagher: ok but SLA doc needs a time number, not just “when metrics look good.”

Aisha Bello: numbers still, but mitigation definition is metric-based so the number means something.

Talia Benson: (tracking) action item from me: we need a final decision for v1 table by Friday so incident-bot + postmortem template aren’t blocked.

Rachel Kim: tier question: do we want different TTM/TTR for Enterprise vs Self-serve? I think yes, but keep it simple:
- Hosted Self-serve: comms are via status page + in-app, less bespoke
- Enterprise (Hosted Enterprise + Dedicated): comms are directly to named contacts + shared Slack channels
TTM might be same, but comms cadence differs.

Dev Patel: +1 to comms cadence being tiered. Otherwise we will miss expectations. Customers mostly ding us for “radio silence” not for not having a perfect fix.

Mina Haddad: routing Sev1: I’m ok with TTM 20m instead of 15m if it’s consistent across routing/runtime. 15m feels tight given detection/declare overhead.

Sean Gallagher: note: we’re also adding “category must be set within 15m of declare” in the IC checklist. If TTM is 15m we’re basically saying “categorize and mitigate by the same time.” That’s rough.

Mateo Alvarez: runtime Sev1: I’d suggest TTM 30m for sure (maybe 45m for some edge cases), but we can commit to 30m if we explicitly allow “mitigate via rollback/fallback” and treat “no rollback path” as escalated.

Priya Natarajan: does it make sense to define two runtime subcategories? e.g., “runtime regression (rollback available)” vs “runtime instability (no safe rollback)”?

Sean Gallagher: that’s starting to drift into too much granularity for v1.

Aisha Bello: compromise proposal (v1):
- Sev1 (Routing/Control plane) TTM: 30m (all tiers)
- Sev1 (Runtime crash/regression) TTM: 30m (all tiers)
- For Enterprise tiers: add explicit comms SLA: initial customer update <= 15m from declare, then every 30m
- TTR targets differ:
  - Routing Sev1 TTR: 72h (3 days) because we can usually fix in config/code quickly
  - Runtime Sev1 TTR: 5 business days because it may require deeper fix + validation

Aisha Bello: reason: align the “stop the bleeding” target across categories so we aren’t arguing in the heat of the moment. We preserve category differences in TTR + ownership + follow-up rigor.

Mina Haddad: I can live with routing TTM 30m though it feels a bit loose. But if comms are 15m and we’re actively mitigating, ok.

Mateo Alvarez: runtime side: +1 to TTR 5bd. Realistically the permanent fix might require repro + canary + multi-arch testing. We should avoid setting ourselves up to fail.

Priya Natarajan: question: for routing TTR 72h, is that calendar hours or business? Incidents happen weekends.

Aisha Bello: I wrote calendar hours (72h). For runtime I wrote business days b/c testing/rollout pipelines. But we can make both business days if we want consistency.

Sean Gallagher: I’d rather keep routing as calendar hours because it’s usually policy/config and the “permanent fix” is often just removing the bad rule. Also, if we break routing on Friday, waiting till Wednesday is not ok.

Rachel Kim: for Enterprise commitments, calendar is what they’ll assume unless stated otherwise. If we say “5 business days” explicitly, ok. Otherwise they’ll interpret as calendar.

Dev Patel: support can explain “business days” if it’s in the playbook, but we need to be explicit in doc.

Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers will also ask “why is runtime fix slower than routing?” We should add a one-liner rationale in the SLA mapping page.

Aisha Bello: can add rationale text:
- Routing: config/policy errors; fix is usually rollback/toggle + small code change; faster validate
- Runtime: kernel/scheduler/model stability; requires perf + correctness validation on GPU types; can’t hotfix as casually

Mina Haddad: also: routing Sev1 should require a follow-up item to add/adjust guardrails in policy validation (linting / staging checks). Otherwise TTR is meaningless.

Sean Gallagher: agreed. Postmortem template already has “what guardrail would have prevented this” section, we can tie it to taxonomy.

Priya Natarajan: what about tier differences in mitigation target? Are we comfortable saying a self-serve Hosted Sev1 also gets 30m mitigation target? That’s a strong internal bar.

Sean Gallagher: we already try to mitigate as fast as possible regardless of tier. It’s ok to keep it consistent; the tier primarily affects comms + escalation.

Rachel Kim: +1. Don’t publish different “we care less about you” targets. Internally, focus on consistent reliability.

Talia Benson: can we lock the v1 decision as:
- Sev1 TTM 30m for both Routing/Control Plane + Runtime Crash/Regression
- Sev1 TTR: Routing 72h (calendar), Runtime 5 business days
- Enterprise comms: initial update <=15m, cadence <=30m
- Add explicit “mitigated = customer-visible success rate/latency returns within defined threshold” definition

Aisha Bello: works for me. I’ll update remediation-sla-mapping draft and share for async 👍

Mina Haddad: 👍

Mateo Alvarez: 👍

Sean Gallagher: 👍. One more note: we should add “if not mitigated by TTM, page secondary escalation (Platform sponsor + Runtime sponsor) automatically” for Sev1. That’s consistent with the “avoid handoff delays” goal.

Priya Natarajan: ok with that. Add to escalation expectations.

Dev Patel: and pls include in support playbook: “if Sev1 and no update in 30m, support can page IC directly / eng-sre” (or whatever route). We keep getting tickets where customers say they got no response.

Sean Gallagher: yes. We’ll route through #oncall + incident bot escalation command.

Aisha Bello: I’ll capture comms SLA as separate section so it’s obvious it’s not the same thing as mitigation.

Talia Benson: great, I’ll note this thread as the decision input for the ADR. next step is email signoff from Neha/Sean/Priya (per earlier ask).
